title: How it works
intro: Three pictures of what we are building, in plain words. Every box says whether it is working, in progress or planned. Anyone can fix the words in dashboard/data/design.json.

legend.working: Built and shown to work. The box says where, for example only in software or only in the simulation.
legend.in-progress: Being built, or built but not yet tried for real.
legend.planned: Agreed or proposed, not started yet.

diagrams.title: The demo in one picture
diagrams.lead: What the judges see at 3 PM, step by step.

nodes.title: 1. A person holds out a can
nodes.text: An empty or foam can, never glass. First live tries are Sunday morning, with a stand-in until Brian arrives.

nodes.title: 2. The camera sees the hand and the can
nodes.text: A small, fast detector, meant to run next to the arm. Tried on recorded data and still photos; not yet on the live camera.

nodes.title: 3. The local brain decides it's safe
nodes.text: Only a steady, offered can gives the arm its turn. An extra hand, a jerk or a camera fault makes it wait.

nodes.title: 4. The arm reaches, closes and takes it
nodes.text: Our guarded routine moves in small steps and checks it is still its turn before each one. Replay only so far.

nodes.title: 5. It pulls back, holding the can
nodes.text: If the person doesn't let go within 10 seconds, it opens and gives the can back.

nodes.title: An operator stays on the e-stop the whole time
nodes.text: The hardware stop button on the arm. Software pauses are extra, never the safety stop. The person is named at the 9 AM standup.

nodes.title: Plan B: the taped mark
nodes.text: If the hand-off isn't 8 of 10 by 11:00, the arm picks the can up from a taped spot on the table instead.

notes: Today a local routine on the station laptop drives the real arm. Dream's AI drives the simulated arms, not the real one.
Only the right arm is used. The left arm missed high on Saturday and has a different claw.

items.text: Meant to run next to the arm. Tried on recorded data and still photos; not yet on the live camera.

items.text: "Seeing beer" on screen during the pitch.

items.label: This dashboard
items.text: Every change, decision and blocker.

nodes.title: Helpers being built
nodes.text: Nice to have, not needed for the 3 PM demo.

items.label: Small edge model
items.text: A tiny AI model for the Jetson that fills in when Dream is slow and helps with the last centimetre. It's trained on our own simulated grasps and scored on 180 tables it never saw. With its help, a slightly-off operator held the cup 162 times instead of 18. Simulation only; not on the Jetson or the real arm yet.

items.label: Robot voice (LiveKit)
items.text: The arms crack short scripted jokes ("Beer me.", "Show-off.") at each step, from recorded audio on a local speaker. They can also stream into a LiveKit room. Tested in replay and on a local test server, not yet on stage. The voice never moves the arm.

glossary.plain: The robot arm, made by MakerMods. We have two; the right one does the demo.
Dream Labs' robot AI in the cloud. Send it camera pictures, get arm moves back. It drives our simulated arms.
Our split: a fast local check decides when the arm may move; Dream or a local routine decides how.
The rule that lets the arm move only on its turn. Anything unexpected, like an extra hand or an old camera picture, makes it wait.
Pausing the arm where it is. It stays powered and keeps its pose. A software pause, not a safety stop.
The hardware emergency stop button. A person keeps a hand on it whenever the arm can move.
A spot taped on the table where the can sits. The backup demo picks the can up from there instead of from a hand.
At 11:00 we count the hand trials: 8 of 10 or better, we demo the hand-off; otherwise the taped mark.
Unreal Engine, the 3D engine that draws our simulated tables.
NVIDIA's physics simulator. It works out what touches what, such as a hand bumping the arm.
A small NVIDIA computer meant to become the arm's own robot server.
A small AI model that runs right next to the arm, so it doesn't need the internet. Fills in when Dream is slow.
A web page that shows what the arm is doing, whether it's healthy, and why it made each decision.
A sponsor's real-time audio and video platform. The robot's voice lines and station events can stream into a LiveKit room so remote teammates can follow along.
